judgement.reason: It praises a teacher who gathered prophetic and apostolic teaching, bearing on the teacher path but not proving a link to Jesus.
It gives one image of Christ, not a full account of who Jesus was.
It tells of Gregory's schooling under Origen, not of how doubt or inability to believe was met.
It speaks of humans being made God, not of Jesus's divine status, and the record forbids using it as a definition of Christ's divinity.
It names the standard doctrine was tested by, not who settled disputes.
It shows a bishop settling a dispute by open argument, with Dionysius's own account as evidence.
It shows God's discipline as aimed at good, but it is Origen's line, not the whole community's.
It shows humility before what he cannot grasp, but about the Apocalypse and not about a personal struggle to believe.
It praises a teacher who gathered teaching into hearers' souls, not an approach to reading texts.
It shows Origen's layered view of Scripture, which is one reader's scheme, not every reader's.
Origen sets the apostolic tradition of the Church as the test of truth, which answers whether other authorities stood beside Scripture.
It tells of a father's arrest and a boy kept at home, not of believers hiding underground.
It shows a bishop putting truth above affection, which bears on authority but not on how it was established.
It shows authority working by patient reasoning but does not say how leadership was established.
It shows one failure toward Origen, told by Eusebius, not how we responded to it.
It speaks of the church's teaching handed down from the apostles, not of rituals.
It says the Word cures the soul's passions, which bears on a troubled mind but is not about a mind that will not settle.
It shows a few practical rulings from the 380s but is not a picture of an ordinary day.
It bears on wealth and detachment but does not say believers had to give anything up.
It reports a failure of the community's own bishop but does not itself say what unsettled anyone.
It shows costly restoration after a fall, a nearby theme rather than an unsettling part of community life.
It says philosophy prepared the Greeks for Christ and says nothing of the eternal fate of outsiders.
